hwinterview-001:
**Key idea:** Pin down the memory *contract* first (depth, width, latency, byte enables, read-during-write and reset behavior), then build an independent reference model that updates **only on accepted writes** and predicts every accepted read. Stimulus covers the address space edges and the ordering cases; assertions and coverage close the gaps.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SEQ["sequences: directed + random"] --> DRV["driver"]
  DRV --> DUT["memory DUT"]
  DUT --> MON["monitor"]
  DRV -.-> IMON["request monitor"]
  IMON -->|accepted writes and reads| REF["reference model (assoc array + valid bits)"]
  REF -->|expected read data| SCB["scoreboard"]
  MON -->|actual read data| SCB
  IMON --> COV["coverage: op x region x mask x collision x reset"]
  SVA["SVA: latency, stable stall, illegal access"] -.-> DUT
```

### Solution
**1. Contract questions to settle before writing a test**

| Item | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Depth/width, address alignment | Defines boundary and illegal-address tests |
| Read latency (fixed / variable) | When the scoreboard expects data |
| Byte enables | Model must merge partial writes |
| Read and write to same address, same cycle | Old data, new data, or undefined |
| Reset | Contents cleared or retained? Outstanding requests dropped? |
| Uninitialized reads | Track "defined" bit instead of assuming 0 |

**2. Test list**
- Address: first, last, every address bit toggled (walking 1/0 on the address), aliasing check (write `A`, read `A ^ (1<<k)`).
- Data: all-0, all-1, checkerboard `0x55/0xAA`, walking ones, address-as-data (catches decoder aliasing).
- Ordering: write-read same address back-to-back, write-write-read, read-write-read, long random mix.
- Multi-port: simultaneous access to same/different addresses, read-during-write on both ports.
- Stalls/backpressure, reset with requests in flight, illegal/out-of-range accesses.

### Code
```systemverilog
class mem_txn extends uvm_sequence_item;
  rand bit        we;
  rand bit [9:0]  addr;
  rand bit [31:0] data;
  rand bit [3:0]  be;
  `uvm_object_utils(mem_txn)
  function new(string name = "mem_txn"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

class mem_scoreboard extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(mem_scoreboard)
  uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(mem_txn) req_f;  // accepted requests, in order
  uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(mem_txn) rsp_f;  // observed read responses
  bit [31:0] model   [bit [9:0]];          // sparse reference memory
  bit [3:0]  written [bit [9:0]];          // per-byte "defined" flags

  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    req_f = new("req_f", this);
    rsp_f = new("rsp_f", this);
  endfunction

  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    mem_txn req, rsp;
    forever begin
      req_f.get(req);
      if (req.we) begin                       // merge byte enables
        if (!model.exists(req.addr)) begin model[req.addr] = '0; written[req.addr] = '0; end
        for (int b = 0; b < 4; b++)
          if (req.be[b]) begin
            model[req.addr][8*b +: 8] = req.data[8*b +: 8];
            written[req.addr][b] = 1'b1;
          end
      end else begin
        rsp_f.get(rsp);                       // in-order read responses assumed
        compare(req.addr, rsp.data);
      end
    end
  endtask

  function void compare(bit [9:0] a, bit [31:0] act);
    for (int b = 0; b < 4; b++) begin
      if (!written.exists(a) || !written[a][b]) continue;   // undefined byte: no check
      if (act[8*b +: 8] !== model[a][8*b +: 8])
        `uvm_error("MEM", $sformatf("addr %0h byte %0d exp %0h act %0h",
                   a, b, model[a][8*b +: 8], act[8*b +: 8]))
    end
  endfunction

  function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    if (req_f.used() || rsp_f.used())
      `uvm_error("MEM", "outstanding requests/responses at end of test")
  endfunction
endclass
```

```systemverilog
a_lat:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reset clears the model **only** if the spec says the memory clears.
- If reads can complete out of order, key the expected queue by tag, not by arrival order.
- A pure-random address stream almost never hits address-aliasing bugs; add address-as-data and walking-address tests.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you know you're done?* Coverage of every address bit 0/1, both boundaries, every collision type, and reset during each in-flight state, with a clean scoreboard.
- *Dual-port same-address write/write?* Spec must define the winner; the model follows the same rule, or flags it as an illegal access.
hwinterview-002:
**Key idea:** Keep a reference priority pointer and predict the winner each cycle. Checks: grant is one-hot or zero, a grant always has a matching request, the pointer moves after each service event, and with all requests held, every requester is served within N service opportunities.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",  "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "req[3:0]", "wave": "=....=..=..", "data": ["1111", "1010", "0001"] },
  { "name": "gnt[3:0]", "wave": "=========..", "data": ["0001", "0010", "0100", "1000", "0001", "0010", "1000", "0010", "0001"] },
  { "name": "ptr",      "wave": "==========.", "data": ["0", "1", "2", "3", "0", "1", "2", "0", "2", "1"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "4-way RR: after granting i, requester i+1 has top priority" } }
```

### Explanation
**Reference model** (pointer = requester with highest priority):
```systemverilog
function automatic int rr_predict(bit [3:0] req, int ptr);
  for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) begin
    int idx = (ptr + k) % 4;
    if (req[idx]) return idx;
  end
  return -1;                       // no request -> no grant
endfunction
// after a grant to w is *accepted*: ptr = (w + 1) % 4
```

**Assertions:**
```systemverilog
a_onehot: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $onehot0(gnt));
a_valid:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (gnt & ~req) == '0);
a_work:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) |req |-> |gnt);
// Fairness: requester 0 held high is granted within 4 grant opportunities
a_fair0:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
            req[0] && !gnt[0] |-> ##[1:4] gnt[0]);
a_hold:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
            gnt[1] && !done |=> gnt[1]);   // grant stable until done, if the spec requires it
```
`a_fair0` uses a cycle bound, which is only valid when each grant finishes in one cycle. With multi-cycle service, count **service events**, not cycles.

**Stimulus:**
| Scenario | What it catches |
| --- | --- |
| All requests held forever | Starvation, pointer not advancing |
| Every 2^N request mask (small N) | Priority calculation errors |
| Request drops before grant | Granting a non-requester |
| Single requester repeatedly | Pointer wrap / stuck priority |
| Requester arrives just after its turn | Correct wait of up to N-1 grants |
| Downstream stall / reset mid-grant | Grant stability, reset pointer value |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Should an idle cycle hold the pointer or reset it? Follow the spec exactly.
- Some designs move the pointer to `winner+1` and others to `ptr+1`. These give different fairness, so the model must match the spec.
- Fixed priority starving a low requester is expected behavior there, not a bug.

### Follow-ups
- *Weighted RR?* Keep a credit counter per requester in the model; check grants are proportional to the weights over a window.
- *Coverage?* Cross winner x request mask x previous winner, plus max-wait histogram bins.
hwinterview-004:
**Key idea:** `type_id::create()` asks the **factory** which class to build, so a test can override it. `new()` calls one specific constructor and bypasses all overrides. Use `create()` for anything a test might want to swap: components, transactions, sequences.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["packet::type_id::create('p')"] --> F{"factory: any override for packet?"}
  F -->|no| P["new packet object"]
  F -->|"yes: packet -> err_packet"| E["new err_packet object (returned as packet handle)"]
  B["new('p')"] --> P2["always packet, overrides ignored"]
```

### Explanation
| | `type_id::create()` | `new()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goes through factory | Yes | No |
| Honors type/instance overrides | Yes | No |
| Requires registration | `` `uvm_object_utils`` / `` `uvm_component_utils`` | No |
| Sets hierarchical name/parent for components | `create("drv", this)` | `new("drv", this)` also does, but no override |
| Typical use | Components, sequence items, sequences | Small helpers, TLM FIFOs, ports, covergroups |

```systemverilog
class packet extends uvm_sequence_item;
  `uvm_object_utils(packet)
  function new(string name = "packet"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

// In a component's build_phase
drv = my_driver::type_id::create("drv", this);   // overridable
p   = packet::type_id::create("p");              // overridable
p   = new("p");                                  // NOT overridable
```

- The factory returns the *derived* object through a *base* handle. Virtual methods give the new behavior.
- `create()` works on the requested type and its registered overrides. Without the registration macro, the class cannot be created by the factory, and string-based lookups (`+uvm_set_type_override`) will not find it.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Overrides must be set **before** the `create()` call. Objects already built are not changed.
- Ports, exports, and analysis FIFOs are normally built with `new()`, which is correct. They are not factory objects.
- The override class must extend the original type. If it doesn't, you get a factory error or a cast failure.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is the constructor signature fixed?* The factory calls `new(name)` for objects and `new(name, parent)` for components, so extra arguments must have defaults.
- *How to debug?* `factory.print()` or `uvm_top.print_topology()` shows active overrides and the real types.
hwinterview-005:
**Key idea:** A **type override** replaces a type everywhere it is created through the factory. An **instance override** replaces it only for a matching hierarchical path. When both match, the instance override wins.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C["base_driver::type_id::create('drv', agent0)"] --> I{"instance override matches path?"}
  I -->|yes| IO["use instance override type"]
  I -->|no| T{"type override for base_driver?"}
  T -->|yes| TO["use type override type"]
  T -->|no| B["use base_driver"]
```

### Explanation
| | Type override | Instance override |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Every factory `create` of that type | Only matching full path (wildcards allowed) |
| API | `set_type_override(new_type)` | `set_inst_override(new_type, "path")` |
| Precedence | Lower | Higher |
| Typical use | "All drivers inject errors" | "Only agent0's driver injects errors" |

```systemverilog
class err_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(err_test)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    // every base_driver in the env becomes error_driver
    base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(error_driver::get_type());
    // but agent1 gets a slow_driver (instance wins over type)
    // path is relative to 'this' (uvm_test_top) when a parent is passed
    base_driver::type_id::set_inst_override(slow_driver::get_type(),
                                            "env.agent1.drv", this);
    super.build_phase(phase);           // env is created after the overrides
  endfunction
endclass
```

Result: `agent0.drv` is `error_driver`, `agent1.drv` is `slow_driver`.

- The path in `set_inst_override(type, path, parent)` is relative to `parent` when one is given (here it becomes `uvm_test_top.env.agent1.drv`). With `parent = null`, pass the full path.
- For objects, the path is the context passed to `create(name, parent, contxt)`. A sequence item created with no context has only a name, so give it a context (for example `get_full_name()`) if you want instance overrides on objects.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Call the override before the target is created. The usual mistake is calling it after `super.build_phase()` when the parent creates the env there.
- A path typo matches nothing and gives no error. Check with `factory.print()`.
- `replace = 0` in `set_type_override` keeps an earlier override in place.

### Follow-ups
- *Command line?* `+uvm_set_type_override=base_driver,error_driver` and `+uvm_set_inst_override=base_driver,slow_driver,uvm_test_top.env.agent1.drv`.
- *Override by name?* `set_type_override_by_name("base_driver","error_driver")`. This works only for registered classes.

**Key idea:** `run_test()`, called from an `initial` block in the top module, starts UVM. It creates the test named by `+UVM_TESTNAME` (or by its string argument) as `uvm_test_top`, runs all phases, and then calls `$finish`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TOP as tb_top module
  participant ROOT as uvm_root
  participant F as factory
  participant T as uvm_test_top
  TOP->>TOP: config_db set vif
  TOP->>ROOT: run_test()
  ROOT->>F: create +UVM_TESTNAME
  F-->>ROOT: my_test instance
  ROOT->>T: build -> connect -> end_of_elab -> start_of_sim
  ROOT->>T: run_phase (objections)
  ROOT->>T: extract -> check -> report -> final
  ROOT->>TOP: $finish
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  `include "uvm_macros.svh"
  logic clk = 0;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;
  bus_if bus(clk);
  dut u_dut(.clk(clk), .bus(bus));

  initial begin
    uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.*", "vif", bus);
    run_test();              // test chosen by +UVM_TESTNAME=my_test
  end
endmodule
```
Simulator: `vsim tb_top +UVM_TESTNAME=my_test +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM`

- If `+UVM_TESTNAME` is given, it overrides the string argument in `run_test("default_test")`.
- The test must be registered with `` `uvm_component_utils`` so the factory can create it by name.
- `run_test` ends only after every phase finishes. By default it calls `$finish` (controlled by `uvm_root::finish_on_completion`).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Set virtual interfaces **before** `run_test()`, or at least before time 0 ends. Build phase runs in the same time step.
- No test name and no argument gives `UVM_FATAL` "No test specified".
- Only call `run_test()` once.

### Follow-ups
- *Where does phase execution start?* `uvm_root::run_test` calls `uvm_phase::m_run_phases()` after it creates the test.
- *Why is it named uvm_test_top?* That fixed instance name gives every config_db/override path a stable root.

**Key idea:** A virtual sequencer is a container of **handles** to real agent sequencers. It has no driver and no items of its own. Virtual sequences run on it so one place can coordinate traffic across agents, for example "program registers over APB, then start AXI data, then poll an interrupt." It is optional: a virtual sequence can also run on `null` with its handles set directly by the test.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  T["test"] -->|"vseq.start(env.vsqr)"| VS["virtual sequencer"]
  VS -->|p_sequencer.apb_sqr| A["APB agent sequencer"] --> AD["APB driver"]
  VS -->|p_sequencer.axi_sqr| X["AXI agent sequencer"] --> XD["AXI driver"]
  VS -->|p_sequencer.irq_sqr| I["IRQ agent sequencer"] --> ID["IRQ driver"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class soc_vsqr extends uvm_sequencer;          // no item type needed
  `uvm_component_utils(soc_vsqr)
  apb_sequencer apb_sqr;
  axi_sequencer axi_sqr;
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
endclass

// env.connect_phase
vsqr.apb_sqr = apb_agt.sqr;
vsqr.axi_sqr = axi_agt.sqr;

class init_then_traffic_vseq extends uvm_sequence;
  `uvm_object_utils(init_then_traffic_vseq)
  `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(soc_vsqr)
  function new(string name = "init_then_traffic_vseq"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    apb_cfg_seq cfg = apb_cfg_seq::type_id::create("cfg");
    axi_rand_seq dat = axi_rand_seq::type_id::create("dat");
    cfg.start(p_sequencer.apb_sqr);       // serial dependency
    dat.start(p_sequencer.axi_sqr);
  endtask
endclass
```

**When you need one**
| Situation | Virtual sequencer? |
| --- | --- |
| Single agent | No |
| Multi-agent, ordering between agents (config before data) | Yes, or a vseq with handles |
| Reusable env where tests should not know the agent paths | Yes, it hides the hierarchy |
| Need to share config/events among coordinated sequences | Convenient place to put them |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Handles must be assigned in `connect_phase`. If they are null, `start()` gives a fatal error.
- `uvm_declare_p_sequencer` does a `$cast`. Starting the vseq on the wrong sequencer type is fatal.
- Calling `start_item` on a virtual sequencer does not work because no driver is connected.

### Follow-ups
- *Vseq on null?* `vseq.apb_sqr = env.apb_agt.sqr; vseq.start(null);`. This works fine, but the sequence can't use `p_sequencer`.
- *Exclusive access?* Use `lock()`/`grab()` on the *real* sequencer for atomic multi-item operations.

**Key idea:** Only `run_phase` and its 12 runtime sub-phases are **tasks**, because they consume simulation time. Every other phase is a zero-time **function**. `check_phase` is a function for end-of-test consistency checks (scoreboard empty, nothing outstanding). It cannot wait, so traffic must be drained before it runs.

| Phase | Kind | Order | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| build_phase | function | top-down | create children, get config |
| connect_phase | function | bottom-up | connect TLM ports |
| end_of_elaboration_phase | function | bottom-up | topology print, sanity |
| start_of_simulation_phase | function | bottom-up | banners, initial config display |
| **run_phase** | **task** | parallel | stimulus, monitoring |
| pre_reset ... post_shutdown (12) | **task** | parallel, in sequence | optional runtime sub-phases |
| extract_phase | function | bottom-up | pull final data from monitors/scoreboards |
| **check_phase** | function | bottom-up | verify end state |
| report_phase | function | bottom-up | print pass/fail summary |
| final_phase | function | top-down | close files |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B["build"] --> C["connect"] --> E["end_of_elab"] --> S["start_of_sim"] --> R["run (task)"] --> X["extract"] --> CK["check"] --> RP["report"] --> FN["final"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  super.check_phase(phase);
  if (exp_q.size() != 0)
    `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("%0d expected items never observed", exp_q.size()))
  if (outstanding_reqs != 0)
    `uvm_error("SCB", "requests still pending at end of test")
endfunction
```

- The ordering is extract (collect) -> check (judge) -> report (print).
- Late responses must be handled in run_phase: keep the objection raised, or use `phase_ready_to_end` / drain time.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A scoreboard that compares in run_phase can still have leftover items. That is exactly what check_phase is for.
- Calling `#` or `@` inside check_phase is a compile error (it is a function).

### Follow-ups
- *Why separate extract and check?* So every component's data is final before anyone judges.
- *Is final_phase guaranteed?* It runs before `$finish` when phasing completes normally.
hwinterview-012:
**Key idea:** Spawn the five workers inside a **supervisor** process. Each worker posts a token to a mailbox when it finishes. After four `get()` calls, `disable fork` kills the supervisor's remaining children only. The mailbox counts correctly even when several workers finish in the same time slot.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as supervisor
  participant W as workers 0..4
  participant M as mailbox done
  S->>W: fork x5 (join_none)
  W->>M: put(2) t=10
  W->>M: put(0) t=15
  W->>M: put(4) t=15
  W->>M: put(1) t=30
  S->>M: get x4 complete
  S->>W: disable fork (kills worker 3)
```

### Solution
```systemverilog
task automatic work(int id);
  #($urandom_range(10, 100));
  $display("[%0t] worker %0d done", $time, id);
endtask

task automatic run_five();
  mailbox #(int) done = new();
  int id;
  fork
    begin : supervisor               // isolates disable fork from caller's other threads
      for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) begin
        automatic int k = i;         // capture loop index per child
        fork
          begin
            work(k);
            done.put(k);
          end
        join_none
      end
      repeat (4) begin
        done.get(id);
        $display("[%0t] got completion from %0d", $time, id);
      end
      disable fork;                  // kill the remaining worker(s)
    end
  join
endtask
```

**Trace example**
| time | event | tokens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | worker 2 done | 1 |
| 15 | workers 0 and 4 done (same slot) | 3 |
| 30 | worker 1 done | 4, then `disable fork` kills worker 3 |

### Explanation
- **Why the outer `fork ... join`?** `disable fork` kills *all* descendants of the calling process. Wrapping the workers in their own process means only the workers are killed, not unrelated threads started by the caller.
- **Why a mailbox and not `count++`?** Either works in practice, since SV threads don't preempt each other. The mailbox, however, lets the supervisor *block* until four are done without polling, and keeps the ids.
- An alternative is `process` handles plus `p[i].kill()` on the one whose `status()` is not `FINISHED`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the fifth worker finishes in the same time slot as the fourth, there may be nothing left to kill. That is fine.
- A killed thread does not run cleanup code. Semaphore keys it held are **not** returned, and objections it raised are not dropped.
- Without `automatic int k`, every worker would see `i == 5`.

### Follow-ups
- *Kill only the slowest?* Same as above, since after 4 completions only the slowest is left.
- *First one to finish wins?* `fork ... join_any; disable fork;` inside an isolating wrapper.
hwinterview-013:
**Key idea:** **Function phases** run in zero simulation time and handle structure: build, connect, and final checks. **Task phases** (`run_phase` and the runtime sub-phases) can consume time with `@`, `#`, and `wait`, and run in parallel in every component. Objections control how long they last.

| | Function phases | Task phases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Examples | build, connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, extract, check, report, final | run_phase; reset/configure/main/shutdown (+pre/post) |
| Consumes time | No | Yes |
| Execution | One component after another (top-down or bottom-up) | All components' tasks forked in parallel |
| Ends when | function returns | all objections dropped (+ drain time) |
| Typical content | create, connect, check end state | drive, monitor, sequences |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph F1["function phases (0 time)"]
    B["build"] --> C["connect"] --> E["end_of_elab"] --> S["start_of_sim"]
  end
  subgraph T1["task phases (time advances)"]
    R["run_phase || reset -> configure -> main -> shutdown"]
  end
  subgraph F2["function phases (0 time)"]
    X["extract"] --> K["check"] --> P["report"] --> Q["final"]
  end
  F1 --> T1 --> F2
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this);       // keep the phase alive
  seq.start(env.agt.sqr);
  phase.drop_objection(this);        // phase ends when the count reaches 0
endtask
```

- A monitor's `forever` loop does **not** keep the phase alive. When the last objection drops, UVM kills all run_phase processes.
- `run_phase` runs **in parallel** with the runtime sub-phases, not before or after them.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- No objection raised means run_phase ends at time 0 and the test passes while doing nothing.
- Raising objections per transaction in the driver works but is slow. Raising them in the test or virtual sequence is typical.
- Use `phase.phase_done.set_drain_time(this, 100ns)` to let in-flight responses finish.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a function phase call a task?* No. A function can't call a task that consumes time (you can fork one, but that's poor practice).
- *Why would you use the sub-phases?* Reset in the middle of a test or phase jumping (`phase.jump(uvm_reset_phase::get())`).

**Classic worked example:** burst of 120 words. Writer: 100 MHz, 1 word every cycle. Reader: 80 MHz, 1 word every cycle.

| quantity | value |
| --- | --- |
| burst write time | 120 / 100 MHz = 1200 ns |
| words read in 1200 ns | 1200 ns x 80 MHz = 96 |
| backlog at end of burst | 120 - 96 = **24** |
| + read start delay (2-FF sync, about 3 rclk) | about 3 words |
| depth to build | 27, rounded up to 32 |

**With idle cycles:** writer 1 word every 2 cycles at 200 MHz (100 Mw/s), reader 1 word every 4 cycles at 320 MHz (80 Mw/s). The effective rates are the same, so the answer is the same 24 words plus margin.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["write rate Rw (words/s)"] --> B["backlog growth = (Rw - Rr) x T_burst"]
  R["read rate Rr (words/s)"] --> B
  B --> M["+ latency margin (sync, startup)"]
  M --> D["depth (round to 2^n for Gray FIFO)"]
```

A small SystemVerilog model to measure peak occupancy for any pattern:
```systemverilog
module fifo_depth_calc;
  timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
  realtime TW = 10ns, TR = 12.5ns;       // 100 MHz writer, 80 MHz reader
  int      BURST = 120, RD_DELAY = 3;    // read starts 3 rclk late (sync latency)
  int      occ = 0, peak = 0, written = 0;

  initial fork
    begin : writer
      repeat (BURST) begin #TW; occ++; written++; if (occ > peak) peak = occ; end
    end
    begin : reader
      #(RD_DELAY * TR);
      forever begin #TR; if (occ > 0) occ--; if (written == BURST && occ == 0) break; end
    end
  join_any
  final $display("peak occupancy = %0d", peak);
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Formula for one burst with the reader running throughout: `depth = B - floor(B * Rr / Rw)` when `Rw > Rr`.
- Back-to-back bursts: if the long-run average write rate exceeds the read rate, **no** finite FIFO is enough. You need backpressure or a guaranteed gap between bursts that lets the FIFO drain.
- Classic trick: "the writer sends 80 words in any 100-cycle window." The worst case is 80 words at the end of one window followed by 80 at the start of the next, so 160 back-to-back writes. Size the FIFO for that 160-word burst.

- Use **word throughput**, not clock frequency, when the interface has idle cycles.
- Async FIFOs need power-of-two depth (Gray pointers), so round up.
- Pessimistic full/empty flags hide 2 to 3 entries of usable space. Add them to the depth.

- *Reader faster than writer?* Depth 1 to 2 is in theory enough. You still need sync margin.
- *Verify it?* Coverage on peak occupancy plus an assertion that `full && push` never happens when no backpressure exists.

| Pulse, fast to slow | pulse stretch | stretch width >= about 1.5 dest periods (known ratio) |

```systemverilog
// Toggle synchronizer for single-cycle events
always_ff @(posedge src_clk) if (src_pulse) src_tog <= ~src_tog;
always_ff @(posedge dst_clk) {dst_q3, dst_q2, dst_q1} <= {dst_q2, dst_q1, src_tog};
assign dst_pulse = dst_q3 ^ dst_q2;         // one dst-cycle pulse per event
```
"Slow to fast" isn't automatically safe. If the clock ratio is close to 1 or the slow clock may run faster in some modes, apply the same analysis.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A toggle loses events if it changes twice before the destination samples it (the two flips cancel). Use a rate limit or a handshake.
- Independently synchronized bits of a bus can arrive in different cycles. That breaks **coherence**.
- Verify with CDC structural tools plus simulation with random phase and jitter, stopped clocks, and resets in each domain.

### Follow-ups
- *How many flops?* 2 is typical. 3 for very high frequency or low-voltage corners (MTBF).
- *Back-to-back pulses fast to slow?* An async FIFO of events, or a counter crossed with Gray code.
hwinterview-055:
**Key idea:** All three keep a wide bus **coherent** by synchronizing only a *control* signal while the data stays stable.
- **Handshake (req/ack):** one word per round trip, with explicit flow control. Good for configuration or status.
- **Recirculation mux:** a synchronized load-enable that selects new data into a destination register (otherwise the register feeds back to itself). It's the capture side of a handshake, not a full protocol.
- **Async FIFO:** buffers many words for continuous streams.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC["source domain"]
    D["data reg (held stable)"]
    REQ["req toggle"]
  end
  subgraph DST["destination domain"]
    S["2-FF sync of req"] --> P["edge detect = load_en"]
    M["recirculation mux"] --> Q["dest data reg"]
    Q --> M
    A["ack"]
  end
  D -->|"wide bus, no sync"| M
  REQ --> S
  P --> M
  P --> A
  A -->|"2-FF sync back"| SRC
```

| | Handshake | Recirculation mux | Async FIFO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Throughput | 1 word per about 4 to 6 slow cycles | same as its control protocol | up to 1 word per cycle |
| Buffering | 1 word | 1 word | depth N |
| Backpressure | ack | needs protocol | full/empty |
| Area | small | small (mux + regs) | RAM + Gray logic |
| Typical use | config, status, rare events | wide registers updated rarely | streaming data |
| Key constraint | data stable from req to ack | data stable while load_en is in flight | Gray-pointer skew, depth sizing |

### Explanation
- In bundled-data schemes the data path has no synchronizer. Correctness relies on the data settling **before** the synchronized control arrives: 2 or more destination cycles later. Constrain the data path with `set_max_delay -datapath_only` so it is shorter than the sync latency.
- Don't reuse the handshake until ack has returned. Otherwise the source changes data mid-capture.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A recirculation mux with no ack-back to the source lets the source overwrite data too early. It needs a protocol around it.
- A reset in one domain alone can leave req/ack half-done. Reset both sides together or design an abort.
- CDC tools must be told about the "qualifier" relation (data qualified by synchronized enable), or they flag every data bit.

### Follow-ups
- *4-phase vs 2-phase handshake?* 4-phase (req high, ack high, req low, ack low) is simpler. 2-phase (toggle) is about twice as fast.
- *Wide counter?* Gray-encode it and use a 2-FF sync. That's coherent with no handshake if it increments by 1.

**Key idea:** **Metastability:** a flop sampled during its setup/hold window can hang near mid-rail for an unbounded (but probabilistically decaying) time. Synchronizer stages add resolution time to reduce failure probability: `MTBF = e^(t_r / tau) / (T_0 * f_clk * f_data)`. They don't remove the effect. **Reset:** assert asynchronously, deassert synchronously in each domain. **Reconvergence:** separately synchronized related signals can arrive one cycle apart, so the logic that recombines them sees an inconsistent state. **Constraints:** CDC and STA setups must describe the same clocks, groups, and exceptions.

```wavedrom
  { "name": "async_d",  "wave": "0.1...." },
  { "name": "ff1",      "wave": "0.x1..." },
  { "name": "ff2",      "wave": "0...1.." },
  { "name": "rst_n_in", "wave": "1.0.1.." },
  { "name": "rst_sync", "wave": "1.0...1" }
],
  "head": { "text": "ff1 may be metastable for a cycle; ff2 output is clean. Reset asserts at once, releases 2 edges later" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Reset synchronizer: async assert, sync deassert
module rst_sync (input logic clk, rst_n_in, output logic rst_n_out);
  logic q1;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n_in)
    if (!rst_n_in) {rst_n_out, q1} <= 2'b00;
    else           {rst_n_out, q1} <= {q1, 1'b1};
endmodule
```

| Topic | Risk | Fix / check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metastability | functional logic sees an unsettled value | 2 to 3 FF sync, no logic between stages, placed close together |
| Reset release | recovery/removal violation, flops leave reset in different cycles | reset synchronizer per domain, recovery/removal timing |
| Reconvergence | `a_sync` and `b_sync` skewed by 1 cycle | cross one encoded signal, or a handshake/FIFO |
| Gray bus skew | multiple bits change at the destination | `set_max_delay -datapath_only` <= 1 source period |
| Constraints | false path hides a real crossing | CDC tool review, matching clock groups, justified waivers |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- RTL simulation can't show analog metastability. Use CDC tools, and optionally inject random 1-cycle delay at synchronizers in simulation to expose reconvergence bugs.
- `set_false_path` only tells STA to ignore a path. It doesn't make the crossing functionally safe.
- Glitchy combinational logic **before** a synchronizer can create pulses the source never meant to send. Register the signal in the source domain first.

### Follow-ups
- *Effect of a 3rd flop?* Adds a full period of resolution time, so MTBF grows by about `e^(T/tau)`.
- *Reset domain crossing (RDC)?* An async reset of one domain can corrupt flops in another domain that sample it. Use isolation or sequenced reset.

**Key idea:** **Setup**: the *latest* data must arrive before the next capture edge minus `t_setup`. **Hold**: the *earliest* data change must arrive after the *same* capture edge plus `t_hold`. Skew (`capture clock arrival - launch clock arrival`) helps setup when positive and hurts hold by the same amount.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "launch clk",  "wave": "p...." },
  { "name": "capture clk", "wave": "p....", "phase": -0.2 },
  { "name": "D at FF2",    "wave": "x.=x.", "data": ["valid window"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "data must be stable from (edge - t_setup) to (edge + t_hold) at the skewed capture edge" } }
```

### Explanation
Same-frequency, single-cycle path:
- **Setup:** `T + skew >= t_cq,max + t_comb,max + t_setup` gives slack `= T + skew - (t_cq + t_comb + t_su)`
- **Hold:** `t_cq,min + t_comb,min >= t_hold + skew`

**Worked example:** `T = 2.0 ns`, `t_cq = 0.15`, `t_setup = 0.10`, `t_hold = 0.05`, `skew = +0.20 ns`

| path | t_comb (max/min) | setup slack | hold slack |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1.60 / 1.60 | 2.0+0.2-(0.15+1.60+0.10) = **+0.35** | (0.15+1.60)-(0.05+0.2) = +1.50 |
| B | 2.10 / 0.02 | 2.2-2.35 = **-0.15** (setup fail) | 0.17-0.25 = **-0.08** (hold fail) |

**Debug flow**
| Violation | Look at | Fixes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup | worst path logic depth, net delay, clock latency | restructure logic, upsize, pipeline, useful skew, slower clock |
| Hold | shortest path, clock skew on capture | insert delay buffers, reduce capture latency |
| Both on same path | large skew | fix the clock tree first |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Lowering frequency does not fix hold.** The hold check doesn't involve the period.
- Setup is checked at slow corners, hold at fast corners, each with OCV derates and clock uncertainty.
- A multicycle path `-setup 2` also moves the hold check unless you add `-hold 1`.
- Hold fixes are mandatory before tape-out. Setup failures only lower the achievable frequency.

### Follow-ups
- *Negative skew?* It hurts setup and helps hold.
- *Why does hold matter for a shift register with no logic?* `t_cq,min` alone has to cover `t_hold + skew`. Clock skew between adjacent flops can break it.
hwinterview-058:
**Key idea:** Crossing AXI between clock domains means crossing **each channel as a stream**. Use an async FIFO per channel (AW, W, B, AR, R), carrying the full payload: id, addr, len, last, strb, resp. Never synchronize individual VALID/READY signals. For two masters sharing one slave, arbitrate AW and AR, **tag** each request with its master (extend the ID), send W beats in the same order as granted AW, and route B/R back by the tag.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M0["master 0"] -->|"AW/AR id=3"| ARB["AW and AR arbiters (RR)"]
  M1["master 1"] -->|"AW/AR id=3"| ARB
  ARB -->|"id = {src, id}: 0_3 / 1_3"| CDC["per-channel async FIFOs"]
  ARB --> WQ["W order queue: grant order of AW"]
  WQ --> WMUX["W mux"]
  M0 --> WMUX
  M1 --> WMUX
  WMUX --> CDC
  CDC --> S["slave (other clock)"]
  S -->|"B / R with {src,id}"| CDC2["async FIFOs back"]
  CDC2 --> DEMUX["route by src bit, strip it"]
  DEMUX --> M0
  DEMUX --> M1
```

### Explanation
- **ID extension:** both masters may use ID 3. Prefixing the source bit keeps them unique and is how responses find their way home.
- **W ordering:** AXI4 has no WID, so write data must follow AW grant order. A small FIFO of granted master numbers drives the W mux. Watch for W arriving **before** AW (allowed). The interconnect must handle or block that case consistently.
- **Bursts:** hold the AW arbitration result until WLAST for the matching burst. Don't interleave W beats from two masters.

**Test list**
| Scenario | Bug it finds |
| --- | --- |
| Both masters same ID, simultaneous | response misrouted |
| Long bursts + random READY on every channel | lost or duplicated beats in FIFOs |
| W before AW, W long after AW | W/AW association |
| Many outstanding reads, OoO slave | ID ordering, R interleave |
| Clock ratios 1:4, 4:1, 1:1 shifted | CDC FIFO full/empty |
| Reset in each domain | hang, orphan responses |
| Fairness under saturation | starvation of one master |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- R beats from different IDs can interleave. RLAST is per ID, not global.
- Exclusive accesses (AxLOCK) need the extended ID to be tracked correctly by the exclusive monitor.

### Follow-ups
- *Scoreboard keying?* Use `{master, direction, id}` with a queue per key.
- *Why not a single FIFO for all channels?* Channels are independent. Coupling them can deadlock (for example, W waiting behind B).

**Key idea:** Decode each **accepted** address against non-overlapping slave windows, save that routing choice for the life of the transaction (all W beats, then B, or all R beats), and return DECERR from a default slave for unmapped addresses. Responses are routed back by the stored master/ID. Register slices must be transparent: same beats, same order, only extra latency.

| Region | Base | Limit | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S0 | 0x0000_0000 | 0x0FFF_FFFF | DDR |
| S1 | 0x4000_0000 | 0x4000_FFFF | SRAM |
| S2 | 0x4001_0000 | 0x4001_0FFF | UART regs |
| none | everything else | | default slave, DECERR |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["master AW/AR"] --> RS1["register slice"] --> DEC{"address decode"}
  DEC -->|S0| S0["DDR"]
  DEC -->|S1| S1["SRAM"]
  DEC -->|S2| S2["UART"]
  DEC -->|unmapped| DS["default slave: DECERR"]
  DEC --> TBL["route table: id -> target"]
  TBL --> WR["W mux and B/R return path"]
```

### Explanation
**Directed address tests:** for each region, hit `base`, `base+1`, `limit-1`, `limit`, `base-1`, and `limit+1` (the neighboring region or unmapped). Also try bursts that end exactly at a limit, and bursts with `len/size` that would cross a 4 KB boundary. Those are illegal for AXI, so the master should never send them. The checker should flag them.

**Checks**
- A transaction reaches **exactly one** target (no fanout unless broadcast is specified).
- The route stays stable while AW/AR is stalled.
- Byte strobes and sideband signals (`id`, `user`, `prot`, `cache`) pass through unchanged.
- End-to-end scoreboard through register slices: count and compare beats in and out, and check that throughput stays at 1 beat per cycle when `ready` is held high (no bubbles).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Overlapping regions in the configuration: decide on priority, or reject the configuration statically.
- A default slave must still consume all W beats of a DECERR write and give exactly one B. It must give `len+1` R beats with RLAST on a read.
- A register slice with registered `ready` needs a 2-entry skid buffer to sustain full throughput.

### Follow-ups
- *Programmable address map?* Randomize the map within legal rules and rerun the same tests. Coverage on every region boundary.
- *Formal?* Prove "decoded target is one-hot" and "route equals the address map" on the decoder in isolation.

**Key idea:** In AXI, the **ID** marks an ordering stream. Transactions with the **same ID** (from the same master, in the same direction) must complete in issue order. Transactions with **different IDs** may complete out of order. A scoreboard therefore needs a queue per `{master, direction, ID}`, not one global FIFO.

```wavedrom

  { "name": "aclk",    "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "ARVALID", "wave": "01..0...." },
  { "name": "ARID",    "wave": "x===x....", "data": ["A", "B", "A"] },
  { "name": "RVALID",  "wave": "0...1..0." },
  { "name": "RID",     "wave": "x...===x.", "data": ["B", "A", "A"] },
  { "name": "RLAST",   "wave": "0...1110." }
],
  "head": { "text": "B (different ID) returns first; the two ID-A reads return in issue order" } }
```

| | Same ID | Different IDs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Response order | in order of issue | any order |
| Read beat interleaving (AXI4) | no, a burst completes before the next same-ID burst | slave may interleave beats of different IDs |
| Throughput | limited by in-order slave | slaves can reorder (DRAM banks) |
| Scoreboard | FIFO per ID | associative array of FIFOs keyed by ID |

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class axi_rd_scb extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(axi_rd_scb)
  axi_txn exp_q[int][$];                      // key = ARID
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  function void write_ar(axi_txn t);          // from AR monitor
    exp_q[t.id].push_back(t);
  endfunction
  function void write_r(axi_txn t);           // completed read burst from R monitor
    axi_txn e;
    if (!exp_q.exists(t.id) || exp_q[t.id].size() == 0)
      `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("unexpected RID %0h", t.id))
    else begin
      e = exp_q[t.id].pop_front();            // must be the oldest of this ID
      if (!e.compare(t)) `uvm_error("SCB", "read data mismatch")
    end
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Read and write channels are independent. Same numeric ID on a read and a write implies **no** order between them.
- Interconnects add master-ID bits. Key the scoreboard on the ID as seen at that interface.
- AXI3 allowed write-data interleaving (WID). AXI4 removed it.

### Follow-ups
- *Need write-then-read order to the same address?* The master must wait for BRESP before issuing the read.
- *Coverage?* Cover out-of-order completion actually happening (response ID differs from the oldest outstanding ID).
hwinterview-061:
**Key idea:** **AXI** is a high-performance, **channel-based** protocol: 5 independent channels (AW, W, B, AR, R), bursts, multiple outstanding transactions with IDs, and out-of-order completion. **APB** is a simple, low-power peripheral bus: one transfer at a time in two phases (SETUP, then ACCESS with optional wait states), with no bursts and no pipelining. A "split transaction" means the request and the response are decoupled, so the bus isn't held while the slave works. AXI does this by design.

| | AXI4 | APB (v2+) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channels | AW, W, B, AR, R (valid/ready each) | single shared address/control/data |
| Outstanding | many, tagged by ID | one |
| Bursts | INCR/WRAP/FIXED, up to 256 beats | none |
| Ordering | in order per ID, out of order across IDs | trivially in order |
| Min cycles per transfer | 1 per beat (pipelined) | 2 (setup + access) |
| Wait states | VALID/READY backpressure | PREADY |
| Error | RRESP/BRESP (SLVERR/DECERR) | PSLVERR |
| Use | memory, DMA, high-bandwidth interconnect | control/status registers |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "PCLK",    "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "PSEL",    "wave": "01...0." },
  { "name": "PENABLE", "wave": "0.1..0." },
  { "name": "PADDR",   "wave": "x=...x.", "data": ["A0"] },
  { "name": "PWRITE",  "wave": "x1...x." },
  { "name": "PREADY",  "wave": "0...10." },
  { "name": "PWDATA",  "wave": "x=...x.", "data": ["D0"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "APB write: SETUP, ACCESS with 2 wait states, completes when PENABLE && PREADY" } }
```

### Explanation
- **APB:** SETUP has `PSEL=1, PENABLE=0`. ACCESS has `PENABLE=1`. The transfer completes on the first ACCESS cycle with `PREADY=1`. Address, control, and write data must stay stable throughout.
- **Split in AXI:** a master issues AR (address accepted) and can then issue more ARs while the first is still pending. The data returns later on R, matched by RID. AHB has a different, explicit **SPLIT** response (AHB2), where the slave releases the bus and calls the master back later.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- AXI-to-APB bridge: verify that bursts are serialized into single APB transfers, byte strobes map to `PSTRB` (APB4), `PSLVERR` maps to `SLVERR`, and AXI backpressure is applied while APB is busy.
- APB assertions: `$rose(PSEL) |-> !PENABLE`, `PSEL && !PENABLE |=> PENABLE`, and address stable while `PSEL && !(PENABLE && PREADY)`.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not use AXI for registers?* Area and power. AXI-Lite is a middle ground (single beats, no IDs).
- *AHB vs AXI?* AHB has one pipelined address/data phase with no separate channels and limited outstanding transactions.

**Key idea:** Reset can delete state that the **other** side still depends on: an accepted address with no data, a partial write burst, or a pending B/R. If only one endpoint resets, the survivor can wait forever. AXI only requires VALIDs to go low during reset. The **system** must define how in-flight work is drained, aborted, or isolated, and verification must prove there is no hang and no illegal protocol behavior across the reset.

```wavedrom

  { "name": "aclk",     "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "s_rst_n",  "wave": "1....0..1.." },
  { "name": "AWVALID",  "wave": "010........" },
  { "name": "WVALID",   "wave": "0.1.|......" },
  { "name": "WLAST",    "wave": "0...|......" },
  { "name": "BVALID",   "wave": "0.........." },
  { "name": "master",   "wave": "x=...=.....", "data": ["burst 2 of 4 beats sent", "waits for B forever (hang)"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "slave reset mid-burst: AW accepted, W incomplete, B never comes" } }
```

### Explanation
**Reset points to test** (random and directed):
| Reset hits | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| before AW/AR accepted | spurious acceptance after reset |
| after AW, before any W | orphan address, W later routed to the wrong burst |
| between W beats | partial write; memory has some beats |
| after WLAST, before B | B lost, master hangs |
| during R burst | RLAST never arrives |
| while READY is low (backpressure) | VALID drops illegally / stale data |

**Checks**
- During reset: `ARESETn == 0 |-> !AWVALID && !WVALID && !ARVALID && !RVALID && !BVALID` (for the side being reset).
- VALID rises only after reset deasserts, synchronously to ACLK.
- A **bounded-completion** watchdog per outstanding ID: B or R must arrive within N cycles, unless the system aborted it.
- The scoreboard tags transactions with a **reset epoch**. On reset, it flushes or reconciles the expected queues, ownership tables, and credits, and doesn't expect old-epoch responses.
- The memory model must not assume a partial burst is atomic, or that it was rolled back.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Partial reset needs a quiesce/isolation protocol: stop new requests, drain outstanding ones, then reset. Or have a bridge return SLVERR for aborted transactions.
- Reset deassertion is asynchronous with respect to the transaction. Randomize its cycle relative to beats.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you find hangs automatically?* Objection timeout plus per-transaction watchdogs that print the oldest outstanding ID.
- *Formal?* Liveness `AWVALID && AWREADY |-> s_eventually BVALID` under fairness assumptions, with reset as an input.

hwinterview-068:
**Key idea:** Every number except one appears **three** times. Count the 1s in each bit position. `count % 3` is that bit of the single number. O(32n) time, O(1) space. A slicker version is a two-variable state machine (`ones`, `twos`) that counts each bit mod 3.

| bit | nums = [2,2,3,2] in binary | count of 1s | mod 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0,0,1,0 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 1,1,1,1 | 4 | 1 |
| result | | | 0b11 = **3** |

### Solution
```python
def single_number(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    res = 0
    for b in range(32):
        cnt = sum((n >> b) & 1 for n in nums) % 3
        if cnt:
            res |= 1 << b
    return res - (1 << 32) if res >= 1 << 31 else res   # restore sign

def single_number_fsm(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    ones = twos = 0
    for n in nums:
        ones = (ones ^ n) & ~twos
        twos = (twos ^ n) & ~ones
    return ones

assert single_number([2, 2, 3, 2]) == 3 == single_number_fsm([2, 2, 3, 2])
assert single_number([0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, -99]) == -99
```

### Explanation
- Per-bit state machine: each bit cycles through `00 -> 01 (ones) -> 10 (twos) -> 00`. After all inputs, `ones` holds the bits seen `1 mod 3` times.
- This is a mod-3 counter per bit, which is easy to describe as hardware.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Python ints are unbounded, so sign handling is needed for negatives in the bit-count version.
- The FSM version doesn't need a sign fix-up, since Python's `~` and `&` act on infinite two's complement.

### Follow-ups
- *Appears k times?* Bit count mod k.
- *Single appears twice, others three times?* With the FSM, return `twos`.

```python
    n = ((n & 0xF0F0F0F0) >> 4) | ((n & 0x0F0F0F0F) << 4)
    n = ((n & 0xCCCCCCCC) >> 2) | ((n & 0x33333333) << 2)
    n = ((n & 0xAAAAAAAA) >> 1) | ((n & 0x55555555) << 1)
```

**Key idea:** The AND of every number in `[left, right]` keeps only the **common binary prefix** of `left` and `right`. Any bit below the first differing bit is 0 for some number in the range. Shift both right until they're equal, then shift back.

| left=5 (101), right=7 (111) | shift | left | right |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| start | 0 | 101 | 111 |
| step 1 | 1 | 10 | 11 |
| step 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 (equal) |
| result | | 1 << 2 = **100 = 4** | |

### Solution
```python

    shift = 0
    while left != right:
        left >>= 1
        right >>= 1
        shift += 1
    return left << shift

def range_bitwise_and_k(left: int, right: int) -> int:   # Kernighan variant
    while right > left:
        right &= right - 1          # clear lowest set bit of right
    return right

assert range_bitwise_and(5, 7) == 4 == range_bitwise_and_k(5, 7)
assert range_bitwise_and(1, 2147483647) == 0
```

### Explanation
- The range from `left` to `right` passes through a carry into the first differing bit, so every lower bit goes through a 0.
- O(log right) time. You don't need to iterate over the range.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `left == right` returns `left`.
- A brute-force loop over the range times out for large ranges.

| nums = [1,2,1,3,2,5] | |

```python
    for n in nums:
        x ^= n
    low = x & -x                      # lowest differing bit
    a = b = 0
    for n in nums:
        if n & low:
            a ^= n
        else:
```

**Key idea:** `n+1` values in `1..n`, so a duplicate must exist (pigeonhole). Treat `i -> nums[i]` as a **linked list**. The duplicate is where two pointers enter the same node, which is the **start of a cycle**. Floyd's tortoise and hare finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space, without modifying the array.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I0["idx 0"] -->|"nums[0]=1"| I1["idx 1"]
  I1 -->|"nums[1]=3"| I3["idx 3"]
  I3 -->|"nums[3]=2"| I2["idx 2"]
  I2 -->|"nums[2]=4"| I4["idx 4"]
  I4 -->|"nums[4]=2"| I2
```
For `nums = [1,3,4,2,2]`, the cycle starts at node **2**, which is the duplicate.

### Solution
```python
def find_duplicate(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    slow = fast = nums[0]
    while True:                       # phase 1: meet inside the cycle
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]
        if slow == fast:
            break
    slow = nums[0]                    # phase 2: find cycle entry
    while slow != fast:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[fast]
    return slow

assert find_duplicate([1, 3, 4, 2, 2]) == 2
assert find_duplicate([3, 1, 3, 4, 2]) == 3
```

### Explanation
- Phase 2 works because the distance from the start to the cycle entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry (mod the cycle length).
- Alternative: binary search on value. Count elements `<= mid`. If the count is greater than `mid`, the duplicate is in `[1, mid]`. That's O(n log n).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The duplicate may appear more than twice. Floyd still works.
- Sorting or marking negatives modifies the input, which the problem forbids.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is index 0 never part of the cycle?* No value equals 0, so nothing points back to index 0. It's a safe starting point.
